summary: Diosmin is a citrus-derived venoactive flavonoid, usually given as micronized purified flavonoid fraction (90% diosmin + 10% hesperidin, MPFF) for chronic venous insufficiency (leg pain, edema, varicose veins) and acute/chronic hemorrhoidal disease. It improves venous tone and lymphatic drainage and reduces capillary permeability. It is NOT FDA-approved; in the US it is sold as a dietary supplement, while in the EU it is an approved prescription/OTC venotonic.
indications: Chronic venous insufficiency / venolymphatic insufficiency (heavy legs, pain, edema, varicose veins)
Symptoms and signs of chronic venous disease (CEAP C0s-C6)

admin: Take orally with meals to reduce GI upset

Use higher loading regimen only for acute hemorrhoidal attacks, then reduce

moa: Diosmin and its aglycone diosmetin prolong the vasoconstrictor effect of norepinephrine on the vein wall, increasing venous tone and reducing venous capacitance and stasis. It also improves lymphatic drainage, decreases capillary hyperpermeability and fragility, and exerts anti-inflammatory effects by reducing leukocyte adhesion/activation and protecting the venous endothelium from microcirculatory injury.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to diosmin, hesperidin or other component
relative: Pregnancy (especially first trimester) due to limited data
monitor: Acute hemorrhoidal symptoms not improving within ~15 days (re-evaluate, exclude other anorectal disease)

preg: Limited human data. Avoid during the first trimester. Animal studies have not shown teratogenicity, but as a precaution use only if clearly needed and after the first trimester when benefit outweighs risk.
lact: Use is not recommended during breastfeeding because data on excretion into human milk are insufficient.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is described; diosmin is largely metabolized and excreted via feces and urine as metabolites.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is established. Use with general caution in significant hepatic impairment given limited data.

minor: Theoretical: flavonoids may modestly inhibit certain CYP/P-gp pathways - clinical relevance unclear
interactions.food: Take with food to improve tolerability; no clinically significant food interaction.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction reported with alcohol.
interactions.diagnostics: No known interference with laboratory tests.

common: Mild GI upset (nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain)
emergency: Angioedema or severe hypersensitivity reaction (very rare)

monitoring: Clinical response of venous symptoms (pain, edema, heaviness) and hemorrhoidal symptoms
Re-evaluate if acute hemorrhoidal symptoms persist beyond ~15 days of treatment
counsel: Take with meals to lessen stomach upset
For chronic venous disease, combine with compression stockings, leg elevation and regular exercise
For a flare of hemorrhoids, follow the short higher-dose course then reduce as directed
Seek medical review if hemorrhoid symptoms do not improve within about 2 weeks or if bleeding occurs - it is not a substitute for evaluation of rectal bleeding
This product is sold as a dietary supplement in the US and is not FDA-approved
pk: Symptomatic relief over days to weeks
Store at room temperature, protect from moisture
pearls: NOT FDA-approved: marketed as a dietary supplement in the US; a prescription/OTC venotonic in the EU and many other countries (use EMA/SmPC and BNF data) - openFDA returns no record
Usually given as micronized purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF): ~90% diosmin + 10% hesperidin (Daflon/Detralex)
Micronization (particle size reduction) increases bioavailability versus plain diosmin
Acute hemorrhoid regimen uses a high loading dose (3,000 mg/day) that tapers over a week
Adjunct only - does not replace compression therapy, lifestyle measures, or work-up of rectal bleeding/varicose veins
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered with food unless it is almost time for the next dose; in that case skip the missed dose. Do not double up.
overdose: No specific antidote. Overdose is expected to be of low toxicity given the favorable safety profile; manage supportively and symptomatically (mainly GI symptoms).
